_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: It is taught in one [baraita]: [This refers] to one who consecrates an ancestral field. “He may borrow and redeem” is the same as what was taught above [30b]: “If he will indeed redeem” teaches that he may borrow and redeem, etc.; and Rabbi Shimon states it. And the other [baraita] is the Rabbis, who disagree with him.
rashi:a2.1: Mishna. He may redeem immediately: and it does not have the law of an ancestral field, where he must wait two years.
rashi:a2.2: This is like a form of interest: for when he returns his money to him within the year, and this one [the buyer] deducts nothing for him, it turns out that he used his house in return for waiting for his money.
rashi:a2.3: And it is not interest: full [interest], for it is called interest only when it comes through a loan, and not through a sale.
rashi:a3.1: His son may redeem: within the year, if he wishes; but after a year it becomes permanent and is never redeemed again, as it is written: “And if it is not redeemed until the passage of a full year for him,” etc. (Leviticus 25:30).
rashi:a3.2: Only from the time that it was sold: for if Reuven sold it to Shimon in Nisan, and Shimon [sold it] to Levi in Iyyar, once the next Nisan arrives it becomes permanent. One does not count for the second sale, but for the first.
rashi:a3.3: As it is stated: “Until the passage of a full year for him”: implying that one counts for this one, whose ancestral holding it was.
rashi:a4.1: The intercalated month: so that if it was a leap year, it does not become permanent until thirteen months [have passed].
rashi:a4.2: A year and its addition: whether in an ordinary year or in a leap year, we give him a lunar year and the days by which the solar year exceeds the lunar year, eleven days, on account of which we intercalate the year.
rashi:a4.3: And one to whom it is given as a gift: if the giver wishes to redeem it within its year, he may redeem it; and if not, it is permanently his [the recipient’s].
rashi:a5.1: Gemara. The mishna: which teaches “he may redeem immediately,” implying that he may redeem it even on the very day he sold it, is not in accordance with Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi].
rashi:a5.2: “For days he shall have the right of redemption,” and “days” are no fewer than two: that it should not remain in the buyer’s hand for less than two days.
rashi:a8.1: And the Rabbis: indeed, that [phrase] is certainly needed for this: “of its sale,” and not the year of the world’s count. And “days” is needed for hour to hour: so that if he sold it on the first of Nisan at midday, one does not count a year for him until midday of the next first of Nisan arrives.
rashi:a9.1: From day to day: that if he sold it on the first of Nisan, one does not count the year by the world’s count, saying that once Tishrei arrives a year has passed for him, since that year has ended. Rather, it does not become permanent until the next first of Nisan.
rashi:a9.2: The year of its sale: and not of the world’s count.
rashi:a11.1: The mishna is Rabbi Yehuda: who says that one-sided interest is permitted. He calls interest that comes through a sale “one side,” because it does not come to interest from both sides: if he does not redeem it and it becomes permanently his, there is no interest here. But a loan certainly comes to interest, since it never becomes permanent [property of the lender].
rashi:a11.2: And made a sale of his field to him: he pledged his field to him for that maneh and wrote to him: If I do not give you a maneh from now until three years, it is yours.
rashi:a11.3: As long as the seller consumes the produce: all those years, it is permitted.
rashi:a11.4: The buyer consumes the produce, prohibited: lest he redeem it within the three [years], and it turns out that he consumed them as interest.
rashi:a12.1: The mishna is Rabbi Yehuda: who says that one-sided interest is permitted. He calls interest that comes through a sale “one side,” because it does not come to interest from both sides: if he does not redeem it and it becomes permanently his, there is no interest here. But a loan certainly comes to interest, since it never becomes permanent. [The same comment appears on the previous segment.]
rashi:a12.2: We read: “An incident involving Baitos ben Zonin.” [This is Rashi’s version of the text.]
rashi:a13.1: One-sided interest: that if he redeems it, it will be interest, and if not, it will not be interest.
tosafot:a1.1: It is taught in one [baraita]: one may borrow and redeem, [and redeem] partially: Rashi explained that it refers to one who consecrates an ancestral field. But this does not seem right to me, for if so, the unattributed mishna [30b] that teaches “but with regard to the Temple, it is permitted in all of them” would follow Rabbi Shimon and not the Rabbis. And the Ri said that it refers to one who sells a house among the houses of walled cities, and so the discussion in the first chapter of Kiddushin (21a, and there 20b) proves. But with regard to one who consecrates an ancestral field, even the Rabbis agree that one may borrow and redeem, and redeem partially.
tosafot:a1.2: It is taught in the Torat Kohanim regarding one who sells an ancestral field: “And he shall reckon the years of its sale” (Leviticus 25:27): you reckon years, but you do not reckon months. And from where [is it derived that] if he wished to make months [count as] a year, he may do so? The verse states: “And he shall reckon.” And if you say: how do we find that both are for the seller’s need, so that there is gain for the seller? Granted, when he reckons months, we find it, e.g., where he comes to redeem it in the middle of the year, that we reckon for him the months that have passed, which the buyer consumed, to reduce his redemption price, just as we reckon the years that have passed, which the buyer consumed. But “you do not reckon months,” how do you find [that this is for his gain]? One can say that you find it, e.g., where he sold in Nisan for ten and a half litra, and there were ten and a half years until the Jubilee, and he comes to redeem it on Rosh HaShana, and there are five more years to come until the Jubilee.
tosafot:a9.1: From day to day and from hour to hour is derived from “until the completion of the year of its sale”: In tractate Niddah (47b, and there, s.v. kulan), Rabbi Elḥanan explained that only with houses of walled cities do we require [a year] from hour to hour; but with the other cases there, where one can say that we follow their own years and not the years of the world, in all of them we do not require hour to hour, for it is only with houses of walled cities that the verse revealed it, and not with the others. And the Tosafot wrote here that the same applies to all of them: we require hour to hour, since we derive “year” “year” from houses of walled cities, as the Gemara says below [31b] with regard to another matter.
tosafot:a10.1: In brief: Rabbi Yoḥanan concludes that the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda, who permits one-sided interest, and the baraita that calls this “full interest” follows the Rabbis. Tosafot ask: how is this different from a mortgage without deduction [mashkanta be-lo nakhyata], which is only “the dust of interest,” as in Bava Metzia 62a, where Ravina says that by their laws one exacts [it] from lender to lender, and by our law one does not return [it] from lender to borrower, so it is not full interest; yet here it is called full interest? According to Rashi’s explanation, which distinguishes between a field and a house, this is resolved. On the mishna in Bava Metzia 64b, “one who lends to another may not live in his courtyard for free nor rent from him for less, because it is interest,” Rashi asked how this differs from a mortgage with deduction, which is permitted, and answered that a field may not produce, but one cannot fail to benefit from living in a house; so even when he deducts from the rent, it is interest. Accordingly, here too a house that he lives in is certainly full interest, while consuming a field’s produce, which may not grow, is not full interest even without deduction. Rabbeinu Tam rejects this distinction, since a house too is uncertain: it may fall or burn. Rather, there is no difference between field and house, and the mishna about renting for less is answered differently: the permitted mortgage with deduction is where he lent against the field, and the borrower could not rent it to another anyway, since it is in the lender’s hand; whereas “he may not rent from him for less” is where he did not lend against the field or the house, and the borrower could rent it to another, so a discount is interest. On Rabbeinu Tam’s view the question returns: why is a mortgage without deduction not considered full interest? One must say that “full interest” here means by rabbinic law, and “but the Torah permitted it” means that by writing the law of houses of walled cities, the Merciful One revealed that in such a case it is not interest by Torah law. tosafot:a13.1: And Rabbi Yehuda holds that one-sided interest is permitted: And if you say: according to Rabbi Yehuda, let a mortgage without deduction also be permitted, since it is one-sided interest, for perhaps he will never redeem it. One can say: we consider it one-sided interest only in a case like “he made a sale of his field to him,” where there is a side of sale if he does not redeem it within the time fixed for him. But a mortgage without deduction has no side of sale, since it is always in the borrower’s power to redeem it; and if he redeems it, since he does not deduct for him the produce he consumed, it is interest. It is just like one who lends a se’a for a se’a, which Rabbi Yehuda does not consider one-sided interest: even though perhaps [the price] will not rise, nevertheless, since there is no side of sale in it, it is prohibited, and Rabbi Yehuda does not consider it one-sided interest.
gershom:a1.1: It is taught in one [baraita]: one may borrow and redeem, and redeem partially: this refers to one who sells a house among the houses of walled cities, for so it is implied in tractate Kiddushin.
gershom:a2.1: This is the Rabbis and that is Rabbi Shimon: the one that teaches “he may borrow and redeem, partially” is Rabbi Shimon. [Just as] he said, “Because we find [that where his power was diminished in one respect, his power was enhanced in another respect],” so here too, [with one who sells a house in a walled city, since his power was diminished,] in that if twelve months arrived and it was not redeemed, it became permanently the buyer’s, his power is enhanced in another respect, in that he may borrow and redeem. And the one that teaches “he may not borrow and redeem” is the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Shimon and do not hold “because we find,” etc.
gershom:a3.1: He may redeem immediately: even right away, when he sold it.
gershom:a4.1: This is like a form of interest: for if it was in the buyer’s hand for half a year [or] eight months, the buyer deducts nothing for the redeemer from what he consumed. And this is like a form of interest, that he takes all his money and deducts nothing for him.
gershom:a5.1: And it is not interest: for he causes him no loss at all, since the Torah granted it to him.
gershom:a6.1: Until the passage of a full year for him: [that is,] for his sale.
gershom:a7.1: A year and its addition: (365; that is, its addition is the eleven days by which the solar year exceeds the lunar year.) That is, the lunar year and the amount by which the months of the sun exceed the months of the moon, eleven days, which makes 365 days, so that it is full both by the moon and by the sun.
gershom:a8.1: The mishna, which teaches “he may redeem immediately,” is not in accordance with Rabbi, as it is taught: “For days he shall have the right of redemption”; Rabbi says: “Days” are no fewer than two. That is, he holds that one who sells a house among the houses of walled cities may not redeem it until after two days.
gershom:a9.1: And the Rabbis: who hold that he may redeem immediately, what do they do with this “days”?
gershom:a10.1: They need it: [to teach] that he may redeem until the passage of a year from day to day. And they need “days” for a full year from hour to hour, [counting to] the same hour at which he sold it.
gershom:a11.1: From “until the completion of the year of its sale”: he derives from day to day and from hour to hour; “days” is left over for him, [to teach] that “days” are no fewer than two.
gershom:a12.1: And not a year of the world’s count: for we do not say that if he sold it to him in Elul or in Av, once the first day of Tishrei arrives a year has passed for him; rather, he counts a complete year.
gershom:a13.1: They need it for hour to hour: that is, if he sold it to him on Passover, and that year Passover fell on the first day of the week, and the next year Passover falls on the fifth day, we do not say that once the first day of the week in the next Nisan arrives, which is the [eleventh] of the month, a year has passed for him [from day to day]; rather, a year has not passed for him until Passover arrives, which is hour to hour.
gershom:a14.1: From day to day and from hour to hour is derived from “until the completion of the year of its sale”: “days” is left over for him, [to teach] that “days” are no fewer than two.
gershom:a15.1: And made a sale of his field to him: when he borrowed from him, he said to him: If I do not repay you from now until such-and-such a time, my field shall be sold to you from now for such-and-such [a price], and you shall reckon your money in it and return to me whatever exceeds your debt. And now it is in the buyer’s possession.
gershom:a16.1: As long as the seller consumes the produce until that time, it is permitted: for until that time it is his.
gershom:a17.1: The buyer consumes the produce, prohibited: for perhaps this one [the borrower] will redeem it, and it will turn out that the buyer consumed interest retroactively.
gershom:a18.1: Rabbi Yehuda says: even when the buyer consumes the produce it is permitted: since he does not hold it as a pledge, but as a sale.
gershom:a19.1: The difference between them is one-sided interest: it is called “one-sided interest” because only the interest of a loan, such as lending a sela for five dinars, is considered [full] interest; but interest through buying and selling is called one-sided interest. And some say: this is one-sided interest, that if he redeems it, what he consumed will be interest, and if he does not redeem it, it will not be interest.
rashi:b1.1: Everyone agrees that one-sided interest: in this way is prohibited, since it originally came into his hand by way of a loan. And where Rabbi Yehuda permits, we are dealing with a case where they stipulated at the outset that if the seller redeems it within the three [years], the buyer will return to him the value of the produce that he consumed; and they disagree about interest on condition that it be returned. And the mishna and the tanna of the baraita disagree about this: our tanna holds that it is not even one-sided [interest], since it came into his hand by way of a sale; and the tanna of the baraita holds that in the end, since it comes to interest, it is one-sided [interest] and is like full interest, except that the Torah permitted it.
rashi:b2.1: (“And if a man sells,” the Merciful One said.)
rashi:b2.2: “And he shall have the right of redemption,” in any case: implying that, if [only the seller could redeem], it should have written “he shall redeem it until the completion of the year of its sale”; since it changed its wording and wrote “and his redemption shall be,” this implies even by another.
rashi:b3.1: “To the one who bought it”: implies that for the buyer it becomes permanent if it is not redeemed within a year; hence, if it is redeemed, he must return it. And it is the buyer who must return it, but not his son. [The verse] teaches us “and he shall have the right of redemption,” in any case.
rashi:b4.1: Year: if it had written “until the passage of a year” and had not written “for him,” I would not know whether [it means] a year for the first sale or a year for the second sale. For example, Reuven sold it to Shimon in Nisan, and Shimon [sold it] to Levi in Tishrei; I would say that Reuven, who sold it first, reckons with Levi and has the right to redeem it until the next Tishrei. Now that it writes “for him,” it implies that it refers back to the first seller.
rashi:b5.1: To whom is it permanent: when a year has arrived for the first seller and it has become permanent, which of the buyers acquires this permanence?
rashi:b5.2: It is permanent for the first: for Reuven can no longer redeem it from Shimon; but Shimon can redeem it from Levi until a year arrives for the second sale, for it has not become permanent for Levi.
rashi:b5.3: It is permanent for the second: for Shimon cannot redeem it from Levi.
rashi:b6.1: A year has passed for him: for there is [a full year] from day to day. But for the one he sold to him on the fifteenth of Adar, a year has not passed for him until the fifteenth of Adar of the next year, even though now it is thirteen months, because we require [a year] from day to day, from the fifteenth of Adar to the fifteenth of Adar.
rashi:b7.1: But let him say: the first buyer to the second buyer: “I preceded [you in] kindling the fire,” I heated and made use of the house before you, yet yours becomes permanent on the first of Adar and mine does not become permanent?
rashi:b7.2: You descended into the intercalation: you entered [the house] in the intercalated month; therefore you lose, for “full” is written, to give him [the seller] the intercalated month. But I did not enter in it.
rashi:b8.1: Two lambs were born to him: and they are firstborns, and he is commanded to offer them within their year, as it is written: “You shall eat it year by year” (Deuteronomy 15:20).
rashi:b10.1: Where “full” is not written: and [one would say] it does not give it the intercalated month, and its year would be completed on the fifteenth of Shevat.
rashi:b11.1: In accordance with the number of days of the sun: whether in an ordinary year or in a leap year.
rashi:b11.2: Twelve months from day to day: as we fix them for a lunar year.
rashi:b11.3: It was intercalated for him: for the seller, since “full” is written.
rashi:b13.1: Doesn’t he say: in tractate Bekhorot, in the last chapter (52b), that a gift is not like a sale, to return in the Jubilee to the one who gave it.
rashi:b14.1: “You shall return”: “you shall return every man to his possession,” and we expound [it there] to include the gift.
rashi:b15.1: And he may always redeem: for it never becomes permanently the Temple’s; and below [the Gemara] explains the reason.
rashi:b15.2: The day of twelve months arrived: [counted] from when he bought it from the treasurer.
rashi:b16.1: Which has no generations: for there is no procreation before Heaven.
rashi:b17.1: Why do I need “it shall not go out in the Jubilee”: since “in perpetuity” is written.
rashi:b18.1: Mishna. Would conceal himself: the buyer, on the day of the twelve months, so that the seller would not find him to give him his money, and it would be permanently his.
rashi:b18.2: That he would place [ḥolesh]: as in “who casts lots [ḥolesh] over the nations” (Isaiah 14:12), and as we read (Shabbat 148b): “One casts lots [ḥalashim] over the sacrificial portions.” That he would cast his money into the chambers that are in the Temple courtyard. [The Davidson English renders “the chamber of the court.”]
rashi:b18.3: And he would break the door: of the house that he sold, and enter.
rashi:b19.1: Gemara. With his consent: that he accepts them willingly.
rashi:b19.2: Against his will: that she threw them into his house, in the same way as Hillel instituted in the mishna.
tosafot:b1.1: Rava said: Everyone agrees that one-sided interest is prohibited: Rashi explained that the mishna and the baraita disagree about this: the tanna of the baraita holds that in the end, since it comes to interest, it is one-sided interest and is like full interest, except that the Torah permitted it; [that is] Rashi’s wording. And one may further explain that the mishna and the baraita disagree about this: for example, where he entered the house [on condition] to return to him the rent for a year if he comes to redeem it within twelve months; the tanna of the mishna holds that interest on condition that it be returned is permitted, and the tanna of the baraita holds that it is prohibited. Alternatively, one [tanna] said one thing and the other said another, and they do not disagree: the mishna speaks of where he returns [the rent] to him if he redeems it, and the baraita of where he does not return it.
tosafot:b13.1: For if it is Rabbi Meir, doesn’t he say that a gift is not like a sale: One can say that since it is not like a sale, it is never in his [the giver’s] power to redeem it, even within twelve months. And according to this, regarding what we asked in chapter HaMakdish (above, Arakhin 28b), that since it is written “for it is their everlasting possession,” we should have said that they may not give their houses as a gift: but we can explain here that a gift is not like a sale, and the giver can always redeem it, even after twelve months. And with this it is resolved that priests and Levites may give their houses to another as a gift.
tosafot:b18.1: In brief: Hillel instituted: this implies that in the days of Hillel, who lived in the Second Temple period (as Shabbat 15a says: Hillel, Shimon, Gamliel and Shimon held their presidency for a hundred years before the Temple’s destruction), the Jubilee was in force, since the law of houses of walled cities was in force, and the previous chapter (Arakhin 29a) says that houses of walled cities apply only when the Jubilee is in force. This is difficult for Rashi’s explanation in Gittin 36a. There the mishna says Hillel instituted the prosbul, and the Gemara asks whether, where the Torah cancels a debt, Hillel could institute that it not be cancelled; it answers that the Sabbatical Year nowadays is rabbinic. Rashi explains there that Hillel holds like Rabbi, that the Sabbatical cancellation of debts nowadays is rabbinic, and that even in the Second Temple period, since the Jubilee was not in force, the Sabbatical Year did not apply by Torah law, and the statement that they counted Jubilees to sanctify Sabbatical Years means by rabbinic law. Yet here it is implied that the Jubilee applied by Torah law in the Second Temple period, and so too in Keritot 11a: on “and they gave their hands to put away their wives, and being guilty…” (Ezra 10:19), Rav Ḥisda says that all of them had relations with a designated maidservant, that is, half maidservant and half free, betrothed to a Hebrew slave; and the previous chapter (29a) says the Hebrew slave applies only when the Jubilee is in force. Evidently they observed Jubilees in the Second Temple period. Tosafot conclude that indeed they did, even though not all of Israel returned in Ezra’s day, as it is written: “The whole congregation together was forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty” (Nehemiah 7:66); some of each tribe returned, and that counts as “all its inhabitants upon it,” as is said below that they counted Jubilees even though not all returned. And Gittin 36a must mean that Hillel did not institute the prosbul for his own generation, but knew that the Temple would be destroyed and therefore instituted it. Although the Gemara there asks whether Hillel instituted the prosbul for his generation or for all generations, that question is asked not according to Abaye but only according to Rava, who answers there that the court’s declaring property ownerless is effective. gershom:b1.1: And here the difference between them is interest on condition that it be returned: that the borrower stipulated with the lender that if he can repay him on time, he will return his field to him. The Rabbis hold that since the borrower stipulated that the field return to his hand, the produce that [the buyer] consumed is interest. And Rabbi Yehuda holds that since he made it a sale to him, the lender acquired it with a complete acquisition until that time, and the buyer is permitted to consume its produce, since it is his; and this return, in which the lender returns it to him, is not like a return but like the lender now selling it back to him. Therefore it is not interest, and the mishna, which teaches “it is not interest,” is Rabbi Yehuda. Another version, in the words of my teacher the Gaon: interest on condition that it be returned means that he stipulated that if he redeems the field, he will credit him the value of the produce he consumed; Rabbi Yehuda holds that since he returns to him the value of the produce, it is permitted.
gershom:b2.1: “And if a man sells,” the Merciful One said, “and he shall have the right of redemption”: that is, [lest you say] the one who sold [is the one who] redeems; it teaches us [otherwise].
gershom:b3.1: Year: as it is written, “And if it is not redeemed until the passage of a full year for him,” I do not know whether [it means] a year for the first or a year for the second. That is, if the buyer sold it to another half a year after he bought it, I do not know whether we follow the passage of the year of the first buyer or of the second buyer.
gershom:b4.1: When it says “until the passage of a year for him,” it speaks of the first seller. To whom is it permanent, if the first seller did not redeem it by the passage of a year? Rabbi Elazar says: it is permanent for the first buyer, for we count for him; for the first buyer we count twelve months; therefore it is right that it be permanently his.
gershom:b5.1: Any right that will come into his hand: that he [the second buyer] stands in his place, so that it becomes permanently his.
gershom:b6.1: A year has passed for him: for he sold on the New Moon of Adar; now, when the New Moon of the next Adar arrived.
gershom:b7.1: But let him say: the one who bought on the fifteenth of the first Adar to the one who bought on the New Moon of the second.
gershom:b8.1: “I preceded you in kindling the fire”: that is, I lit a fire in my house, in my hearth, before you lit [one] in your house, for I bought first. Why does your house become permanently yours before mine, which I bought first, becomes permanent?
gershom:b9.1: For he says to him: “You descended into the intercalation”: you bought in the intercalated month, on the fifteenth of the first Adar; you revealed your intent that you want to reckon a leap year. Therefore its year is not completed until the fifteenth of Adar.
gershom:b10.1: Two lambs were born to him: to know which of them has the status of a ram before the other. And some say [it concerns] combining [lambs] into one pen for the animal tithe, as it is written regarding the animal tithe: “that which comes forth from the field year by year” (Deuteronomy 14:22). [The note ends with an abbreviation, למ״ה, whose meaning is unclear.]
gershom:b11.1: There, where “full” is written: regarding houses of walled cities, to include the intercalated month.
gershom:b12.1: It teaches us that “year” “year” are derived from one another: “year” is written regarding walled cities, and “year” is written regarding lambs: “a lamb without blemish, a male of the first year” (Exodus 12:5). Just as there [it is] “full,” so that where he descended into the intercalation we reckon a leap year for him, so too here.
gershom:b13.1: A year and its addition: that is, the lunar year and the amount by which the months of the sun exceed those of the moon, eleven days, which makes 365 days, so that it is full both by the moon and by the sun.
gershom:b14.1: And one to whom it is given as a gift: the giver of the gift could redeem it for all twelve months, and when twelve months arrived and it had not been redeemed, it became permanently his [the recipient’s].
gershom:b15.1: As it is stated “latzemitut”: it could have said “litzmut,” but said “latzemitut,” to include a gift, that it becomes permanent and does not go out in the Jubilee, like a sale.
gershom:b16.1: In accordance with whom? Not in accordance with Rabbi Meir, who says in chapter Yesh Bekhor LeNaḥala: “These do not return in the Jubilee,” etc. Just as Rabbi Meir holds that a gift is not like a sale with regard to going out in the Jubilee, so too it is not like a sale with regard to becoming permanent.
gershom:b17.1: For the Merciful One included [the gift] with “latzemitut”: as was said above, “tzemit,” “tzemitut.”
gershom:b18.1: The Sages said to Rav Pappa: but we said there, in chapter Yesh Bekhor, that regarding the Jubilee it is written “you shall return” to include gifts, and Rabbi Meir does not include [them], for “tashuv,” “tashuvu” does not imply [to include] to him. So too “tzemit,” “tzemitut” does not imply to him [to include the gift]. Rather, it is certainly not in accordance with Rabbi Meir.
gershom:b19.1: And he may always redeem: for it does not go out to the priests in the Jubilee like an ancestral field.
gershom:b20.1: Another redeemed it from the Temple: that other has the status of a buyer, so that if the day of twelve months arrived and the consecrator did not redeem it, it becomes permanently [the property of] the one who redeemed it from the Temple.
gershom:b21.1: And let the Temple make it permanent: and let it be permanently the Temple’s if it is not redeemed within its year; why may he always redeem it?
gershom:b22.1: The verse states: “Throughout his generations”: for one who has offspring [generations], it goes out in perpetuity.
gershom:b23.1: (Another redeemed it: as it is written: “Shall stand, the house,” etc.
gershom:b24.1: And the other: as it is written: “Shall stand, the house,” etc.)
gershom:b25.1: “It shall not go out in the Jubilee,” that it does not return to the owners: why do I need it?
gershom:b26.1: It might enter your mind to say it should go out in the Jubilee: for the Jubilee cancels his acquisition; it teaches us that it does not.
gershom:b27.1: The buyer would conceal himself: on the day of the twelve months, so that the seller would not find him to redeem it from him, so that it would become permanently his.
gershom:b28.1: That he would place [ḥolesh] his money in the chamber: [the one] made for that purpose; he would put the money [of his redemption] in that chamber when he could not find the buyer.
gershom:b29.1: And he would break the door: the entrance of the house he sold, and enter it; and when the other, the buyer, wishes, he will come and take his money from the chamber.
gershom:b30.1: From Hillel’s enactment, conclude that giving against his will is, in general, not giving.
